text: "Generative Caring" Psychotherapy for Patients Who Are Reluctant to Talk IRWIN N. HASSENFELD, M.D.* Patients seek psychotherapy for relief of symptoms and resolution of problems in living. Yet, they sometimes balk at the prospect of having to choose a topic without being prompted by therapist questions. This paper suggests that this apparently self-sabotaging behavior represents an acting out of a fundamental existential dilemma for many individuals, i.e., to be or not to be an adult. Adulthood comes with the heavy burden of responsibility for making life choices, and the possibility of making the wrong choices. The psychotherapeu- tic situation, with its demand that the patient choose a topic, is a microcosm of the adult-adult relationship. The author proposes that the proper treatment for these patients is Generative Caring Psychotherapy, which promotes emotional growth and facilitates patients' transition from childhood depen- dence to adult responsibility. When a patient refuses to work in psychotherapy, or attempts to sabotage the psychotherapeutic situation, it is thought that the patient's unconscious wishes or fears are working at cross-purposes with his conscious wish to be helped. The two most common explanations for what these unconscious wishes and fears might be are: 1. the fear of recovering unacceptable repressed memories, feelings, impulses (1), or internal objects (2), and 2. the wish to avoid change in order that everything remain predictably the same (3, p. 4). This paper proposes a third explanation which builds on and extends both of the first two. GROWTH AND CARE Emotional growth consists largely of movement from childhood depen- dence on caregivers to taking on responsibility for oneself This process of growth varies from individual to individual; in some people it is very limited. Psychologically, separation from caregiver(s) starts at the moment of birth, perhaps earlier, and continues, mostly in spurts, throughout life, with a major spurt during adolescence and young adulthood. But even under the most propitious of circumstances, the child has lingering doubts *Emeritus Professor of Psychiatry, Albany Medical College. Mailing address: 18 Wilshire Drive, Delmar, NY 12054. AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY, Vol. 53, No. 4, Fall 1999 495 AMERICAN JOURNAL OE PSYCHOTHERAPY about the merits of tnoving from childhood into adulthood. This is because taking care of oneself can be so burdensome, and being taken care of can be so pleasurable. Yet for many, the care and protection they received as children have, in actuality, been fraught with serious lapses, both inten- tional and unintentional. The recipients of poor, inconsistent, distorted, abusive, or incomplete care become adults, who are left with unconscious wishes to find proper care (in accordance with whatever their fantasy of care happens to be). These wishes are expressed in the repetition compul- sion (3, pp. 22, 23) as reenactments of childhood primary relationships in current interpersonal contexts. Most often these reenactments take place in those relationships that most closely resemble the individual's early family situation. Marriage is a likely venue for these reenactments. Any "helping" relationship is fertile ground. Of particular interest to the readers of this journal is the relationship between psychotherapist and patient. THERAPY AS A MICROCOSM OF FAMILY LIFE The psychotherapeutic situation resembles that of the nuclear family. Patients find themselves locked in a struggle with internal representations of their parents and, transferentially, with their therapists. They feel caught between two contradictory wishes: 1. the wish to do the work of therapy and thereby increase their autonomy by becoming more responsible for themselves, and 2. the wish to remain a child and thereby attain the cared-for state about which they fantasize and for which they yearn. After several years of therapy, this was clearly expressed by one of my patients. Mr. A., a practicing attorney. Mr. A. described how in his fantasy he sees himself lying in bed, being fed intravenously, surrounded by family who are all looking intently at him. Another patient's statement illustrates how she played out both sides of her ambivalence about responsibility in one therapy session: Ms. B. [opening the session]: I couldn't wait to come today and get your advice. Later in the session the patient described how infuriated she became when her father told her what to do and how to behave. A common instance of child-parent reenactment occurs in psychody- namic psychotherapy, when a patient seems unable or unwilling to decide what to talk about. This most often happens in the beginning portion of therapy. The patient appears to run out of things to talk about, and, in one form or another, asks for help from the therapist in continuing the dialogue. Some patients can be cajoled into talking; others resist vigorously. Ms. C. requested that her therapist start the hour by talking about himself. When 496 "Generative Caring" Psychotherapy the therapist gently refused and maintained a listening posture, the patient threatened him with bodily harm. Here are a few less extreme and more typical examples of patients who are reluctant to do the work of therapy: Ms. D.: There is no way I can fill a whole session by myself. Mr. E.: Well, that's it. I have nothing else to report. Mr. F.: I don't know what to talk about .. . I'm lost .. . Please ask me a question. Traditionally, this kind of patient behavior is referred to as resistance. My observations have been that this type of "resistance" may occur as early as the first psychotherapy session, before the return of repressed material (4) would be expected to pose a danger, and before the possibility of change looms as much of a threat, both of which, had they pertained, might require drastic defensive maneuvers by patients. These observations have led me to take a fresh look at the behaviors in question and, in turn, the psychotherapeutic enterprise as a whole. As a result, I have arrived at a somewhat different view of psychodynamic psychotherapy, its goals and its methods. THE FLIGHT FROM RESPONSIBILITY By refusing to choose what they will talk about, as they are invited, indeed required, to do, patients attempt to evade taking responsibility for the part of the therapeutic contract to which they have previously agreed. At the same time they pressure the therapist to take over these responsibilities. These patients seek guidance, direction, and advice from therapists on how to live their lives. Unfortunately, in too many cases they get it. By these efforts patients keep alive the fantasy that, if they can only persuade their psychotherapist to stop analyzing and to start taking care of them, they would become happy and fulfilled persons. With surprising tenacity, energy, and guile, patients urge, even bully and seduce their therapists into giving up the therapeutic stance and replacing it with that of friend, coach, guide, advisor, or lover. The burden of adult responsibility, symbolized by the demand in psychotherapy that patients, not therapists, must decide what to talk about, weighs heavily upon these patients. The following vignette illustrates this sometimes unremitting patient quest: Ms. G. [pauses and then says]: I don't know where to go from here .. . I just don't know what to talk ahout... I'm lost... won't you help me out? After the session had officially ended she asked, in a "doorknob" comment: "WeU, what shall I do for homework?" 497 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY NOVICE THERAPISTS' RESPONSES Faced with patients who stop talking, novices explain for the second, third, or fourth time how psychodynamic psychotherapy works. When this strategy does not work, they remain unempathically silent. Usually, as a result, both patient and therapist become more and more uncomfortable. Another novice strategy is to mechanically reflect back their patients' request for rescue, or to ask them why they made the request. None of these strategies are effective. They all reflect the therapist's insecurity, are unem- pathic, and, most important, move the therapist away from the therapeutic posture of empathic listening. EXPERIENCED THERAPISTS' RESPONSES Among responses to patients who try to get their therapist to structure the therapy session or self-disclose—strategies designed to unload their respon- sibilities onto therapists—there are two appropriate responses: 1. Consider the patients' requests to be accurate expressions of their legitimate needs, and give them what they ask for, within the bounds of professional conduct; and 2. meet patients' requests with empathy for their wishes and felt needs for advice, guidance, direction, and structure, but do not grant their request(s). Each response is appropriate in some circumstances and inappropriate in others. Each response has consequences that facilitate or retard emo- tional growth. The first response is appropriate with patients who have serious ego deficits and/or severe defects in the structure of the self. It is, however, recommended by authors who believe that all effective therapy requires self-disclosure and the use of "the authentic self" in a "real" relationship (5). Although I agree with these authors' point that sterile, impersonal, nonspontaneous behavior on the part of a therapist is unpro- ductive, I fear that therapist self-disclosure will collude with the patient's wish to avoid having to take responsibility for choosing a topic. The first response sides with the patient's wish to remain a child and stunts emotional growth. It results in short-term patient satisfaction, but long-term anger at being infantilized. The second response sides with the patient's wish to act responsibly. It promotes emotional growth, autonomy, and individuation. "GENERATIVE CARING" PSYCHOTHERAPY The therapeutic approach described above constitutes the nucleus of a type of psychodynamically based psychotherapy that I am tentatively calling Generative Caring Psychotherapy. It is generative (6) because it promotes patient emotional growth. It is caring because it provides age- 498 "Generative Caring" Psychotherapy appropriate support while increasing patients' freedom to choose. It deemphasizes parent-child interaction, while encouraging adult-adult com- munication. The following three examples give the flavor of this kind of psychotherapy. Mr. H.: [Initial greeting followed by 15 minute silence] You therapists never say anything. Th: It would be a big relief if I did. [long silence] Mr. H.: I guess I'm angry, but I don't know why; I should try to figure it out. Ms. L: [long sUence] I'm not a good conversationalist. Th: It must be hard for you in social situations. Ms. L: Yes [tearful], I can't think of anything to say [silence] I wish my mother would call me [silence]. When I call her she only talks about my brother who lives with her .. . she never asks about me and my daughter. Ms. J., a college student, wished to take time off because college was too hard, especially when she had to choose courses. Ms. J.: Yesterday, I was stung by a bee. Th: That must have really hurt. Ms. J.: [silence] My kid brother started in a special program for learning disabled students. . . . He needs direction and guidance and he isn't getting it there. Th: I wonder whether you feel you would like more direction and guidance here, from me. Ms. J.: [tearful] I wish I didn't have to do everything for myself; sometimes I want someone to take care of me. My mother was a party girl. She never looked out for us. CONCLUSION In Generative Caring Psychotherapy, personal growth is the primary goal; helping patients move from childhood dependence to adult responsi- bility is the objective. The method consists of maintaining a consistent therapeutic posture. This posture is designed to make patients feel that they are being seen, listened to, understood, and affirmed. Toward this end the generative caring psychotherapist does not ask questions unless it is absolutely necessary; abstains from giving advice, direction, and guidance; gives only empathy; accepts no gifts; holds patients responsible for their behavior; maintains the therapeutic frame (7); is aware of countertransfer- ence; and owns up to his or her mistakes.
